bib.title: When is Tree Search Useful for LLM Planning? It Depends on the Discriminator

question: How does the accuracy of an LLM-based discriminator affect language agents using re-ranking, iterative correction or tree search, and can current LLM discriminators meet the needs of advanced planning?
hypothesis: The discriminator may be the deciding factor in agent performance, more than the planning method.
contributions: A unified generator-discriminator-planning-method framework for language agents
Oracle simulation showing discrimination accuracy strongly correlates with agent performance for all three planning methods
Environmental observations (executability check, execution result) that improve LLM discriminators by up to 30.2 points
End-to-end evaluation showing advanced planning gives no significant gain over re-ranking with LLM discriminators, and tree search is 10-20x slower

method.summary: A CodeLlama-13B-Instruct generator samples programs; a discriminator scores them as P(Yes) for 'is the program correct'. Re-ranking, iterative correction (up to 10 rounds) and a heap-based MCTS tree search are compared with oracle-simulated discriminators (accuracy capped by tau) and real LLM discriminators, on text-to-SQL (Spider, Bird) and GSM8K program-of-thought.
method.task: text-to-SQL parsing and mathematical reasoning (program of thoughts); planning with a generator and discriminator

datasets.name: Spider
datasets.size: 400 dev examples evaluated (100 per difficulty level, 4 levels); full training split used for prompting/fine-tuning
datasets.split: random database then example per difficulty level

datasets.name: Bird
datasets.size: 300 dev examples evaluated (100 per difficulty level, 3 levels); full training split used minus database retail_world
datasets.preprocessing: excluded retail_world training examples for annotation errors

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.size: 500 random dev examples (tree search on 100 of them)
datasets.preprocessing: no fine-tuning: training set has no program-of-thought annotation

datasets.name: Intrinsic evaluation sets
datasets.split: built from tau=1.0 re-ranking generations, relabelled

datasets.name: Discriminator training data
datasets.size: wrong SQL synthesised by 2-fold cross-validation on training sets; GSM8K: two hand-annotated wrong programs for the two prompt examples

other.use: generator in all experiments; also discriminator

training.objective: classify program correctness by generating one token, Yes or No
training.regularisation: LoRA (Hu et al., 2022); rank/alpha not stated
training.hardware: up to four NVIDIA RTX A6000 48GB (Spider, GSM8K); up to four A100 80GB (Bird)

inference.samples: 5 sequences per step/problem (num_return_sequences=5); single run, no seeds stated
inference.prompting: Generator: 1-shot BM25-retrieved example (SQL), fixed 2-shot (GSM8K, from Ni et al. 2023b). Iterative correction revision: 0-shot. Discriminator: same shot setup, Yes/No question; fine-tuned ones use no in-context example
inference.retrieval: BM25 for in-context examples (Robertson and Zaragoza 2009)

parameters.tree_search_step: one SQL clause or one line of Python
parameters.tree_search_termination: stop when a complete plan is in the heap
parameters.tree_search_step_score: max over Monte-Carlo simulations from the step
parameters.oracle_tau: probability tau of returning score s, else 1-s; tau swept up to 1.0 (0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0 named in text)
parameters.gpt_score: P(Yes) from top-5 logprobs; 1-P(No) if Yes missing; 0 if both missing

metrics.name: Execution accuracy / answer accuracy
metrics.definition: end-to-end correctness of final plan (SQL execution or GSM8K answer)

metrics.name: Discrimination accuracy (Acc)
metrics.definition: % of correct/wrong pairs where correct program scores higher

metrics.name: Classification macro F1
metrics.definition: macro F1 over correct and wrong classes

metrics.name: Hit@1
metrics.definition: % of batches whose top-scoring candidate is correct

metrics.name: MRR
metrics.definition: mean reciprocal rank of highest-ranking correct program in batch

eval.protocol: Single run; exact McNemar's test (p<0.05) between planning methods with the same discriminator; no seeds or confidence intervals.

prompts.text: Answer the following Yes/No question: Is the SQL correct given the utterance?
prompts.where: Table D.3 (full prompt with correct/wrong example pair)

prompts.text: Answer the following Yes/No question: Is the SQL correct given the utterance and its result?
Given database schema and a question in natural language, correct the buggy SQL query and generate a fixed SQL query.
Given database schema and a question in natural language, generate the corresponding SQL query.
## Answer the following Yes/No question: Is the python program correct given the problem in the comment?
## Given the question in the comment, correct the buggy python program and generate a fixed python program to produce the correct answer with the 'answer' variable.

results.claim: Advanced planning methods (iterative correction, tree search) need discriminators of at least 90% accuracy to significantly beat re-ranking.
results.setup: Oracle-simulated discriminator with accuracy threshold tau; Spider, Bird, GSM8K; CodeLlama-13B-Instruct generator, 5 samples
results.quote: advanced planning methods demand discriminators with at least 90% accuracy to achieve significant improvements over re-ranking

results.claim: Tree search is at least 10-20 times slower than re-ranking and iterative correction.
results.setup: Oracle simulation, all three datasets; slowness mainly from Monte-Carlo simulations
results.quote: tree search is at least 10–20 times slower but leads to negligible performance gains

results.claim: Environmental observations (executability check plus execution result) raise CodeLlama-13B discrimination accuracy on Bird by 30.2 points.
results.quote: we improve the discrimination accuracy of LLMs by up to 30.2 and 8.4 absolute points on text-to-SQL parsing and mathematical reasoning, respectively

results.claim: CodeLlama-13B-FT with observations is best on Spider with re-ranking, 70.3 execution accuracy, versus 62.3 greedy.
results.setup: Spider 400-example dev subset, re-ranking, CodeLlama-13B-FT enhanced discriminator

results.claim: With the best naive discriminator, re-ranking on Spider (61.5) stays below greedy generation (62.3).
results.quote: has the best accuracy (61.5), which is still lower than greedy generation (62.3)

results.claim: With an oracle discriminator (tau=1.0) on Spider, tree search reaches 76.2 and iterative correction 76.0 versus 71.0 for re-ranking.
results.table: Table 3, row Oracle Simulation (τ = 1.0), column Spider Tree Search

results.claim: Only with the oracle does any advanced method significantly beat re-ranking on text-to-SQL; no non-oracle discriminator does.
results.quote: We only observe such improvement with the oracle discriminator.

results.claim: Tree search with CodeLlama-13B-FT enhanced is worse than re-ranking on Spider (67.5 vs 70.3) and Bird (21.7 vs 23.7).
results.quote: (Table 3: 67.5 vs 70.3 on Spider; 21.7 vs 23.7 on Bird)

results.claim: In 25 of 50 sampled wrong pairs on Bird, CodeLlama-13B scores a non-executable SQL query higher.
results.setup: Error analysis, 50 sampled incorrect pairs, Bird intrinsic set
results.quote: In 25 of the 50 pairs (50%), CodeLlama-13B assigns a higher score to non-executable SQL queries.

results.claim: Naive GPT-4-Turbo discrimination accuracy on GSM8K is 93.8, the highest of all discriminators.
results.table: Table 1, row GPT-4-Turbo, column GSM8K Acc

results.claim: Naive GPT-4-Turbo discrimination accuracy on Spider is 76.5 and on Bird 76.2.
results.table: Table 1, row GPT-4-Turbo, column Spider Acc

results.claim: GPT-3.5-Turbo with executability check and execution result reaches 89.2 discrimination accuracy on Bird, from 64.3.
results.table: Table 2, row ++ Execution Result, column GPT-3.5-Turbo Bird

results.claim: Tree search takes 296.0 s per Bird example against 17.3 s for re-ranking with naive CodeLlama-13B.
results.table: Table 4, row CodeLlama-13B, column Tree Search

results.claim: Executability check cuts tree-search latency on Bird by 142.4 s with GPT-3.5-Turbo.
results.table: Table 4, row GPT-3.5-TurboE, column Tree Search

results.claim: Iterative correction with CodeLlama-13B judging its own output gets only 10.2 on GSM8K, versus 39.4 greedy, because revisions turn into non-executable natural language that scores high.
results.setup: GSM8K 500 examples, CodeLlama-13B as generator and discriminator
results.quote: our iterative correction agent only has 10.2 answer accuracy

results.claim: On GSM8K tree search with GPT-3.5-TurboE gets 51.0 versus 47.6 re-ranking, not significant.
results.setup: Tree search on only 100 of the 500 examples
results.table: Table 5, row GPT-3.5-TurboE, column Tree Search

results.claim: Oracle tree search on GSM8K reaches 73.0 vs re-ranking 64.1, still not significant by McNemar.
results.setup: Oracle tau=1.0, tree search on 100 examples
results.table: Table 5, row Oracle Simulation, column Tree Search

results.claim: Discrimination errors dominate failures of advanced methods: 29 of 37 (78.4%) for iterative correction on Spider.
results.setup: Cases where re-ranking is correct but iterative correction is not; CodeLlama-13B-FTE on Spider
results.table: Table 6, row Discrimination, column Spider Iter. Correct.

results.claim: In 15 of the 29 Spider discrimination errors iterative correction had already found the correct SQL but overwrote it.
results.quote: iterative correction has already found the correct SQL queries for 15 (40.5% of the total 37 errors)

results.claim: Search instability: in 12 of 25 Bird cases where iterative correction succeeded and tree search failed, tree search could not choose among tied scores.
results.setup: Bird, oracle tau=1.0; IC 32.7 vs TS 29.3, McNemar p>0.05
results.quote: In 12 out of the 25 examples (48%), tree search fails

results.claim: Tree search consistently underperforms the other two planning methods when tau is 0.8 or lower.
results.quote: tree search agents consistently underperform the other two when the discrimination accuracy threshold τ ≤0.8

results.claim: About 80% discrimination accuracy is needed before agents beat greedy generation on text-to-SQL.

limits: Only instruction-tuned code LLMs (CodeLlama generator) tested; other generators and instruction-tuning effect not ablated (authors).
Only formal-language plans (programs); natural-language plans not studied (authors).
Generator perplexity excluded from scoring; generator influence on planning not studied (authors).
Tree search on GSM8K evaluated on only 100 examples; McNemar often non-significant at these sample sizes.
Single run with one sampling configuration (5 samples, T=0.6); tree-search MCTS implementation is one variant and unstable early with tied scores.
Fine-tuned discriminators not available for GSM8K; GPT-4-Turbo used only in intrinsic eval.
Models (CodeLlama, GPT-3.5/4-Turbo 1106) have since dated; the 90% threshold is from oracle simulation with random label flipping, which may not reflect structured LLM errors.
Evaluation subsets are difficulty-balanced so absolute scores are below standard dev-set numbers.

terms.definition: percentage of correct/wrong program pairs where the correct program obtains a higher discrimination score
The discriminator assigns a higher score for wrong programs than correct ones, which is not recoverable by any planning method.
The planning method has not found the correct program before termination.
